The head stores the ledger and does random spot‑checks, counting the fish on the nets and comparing with the recorded numbers. At the end of the week the council reviews the ledger to make sure no one has taken more than they need. Anyone who misreports will be asked to return the excess fish. This system lets us verify and enforce the catch limits while keeping records in a single place.

agent_2.question: How is a fisher’s personal consumption need defined and determined for the purpose of setting the maximum amount of fish that may be kept?
agent_2.answer: In this lake we have agreed that each of us needs about one unit of fish per day to keep our family alive and healthy. That one unit is what we call the personal consumption need. It is set by a simple community agreement – we look at the daily food we need and decide that one unit is enough to feed one person for a day. Because of that, the ledger we keep at the dock records how much each person catches each day. To figure out how much you can keep, we multiply the one‑unit‑per‑day figure by the number of people in your household and the number of days you fish. The ledger is signed by the fisherman and checked by the village head to make sure that nobody keeps more than that amount.\n\nSo the personal consumption need is: 1 unit of fish per person per day. It is determined by a communal consensus on what is necessary for survival, and is verified by the daily ledger entries.

agent_4.question: How will fishing licences be issued and revoked, and what authority does a 24‑hour licence suspension carry in practice?
agent_4.answer:
The Log‑Keeper will hand every villager a small paper card – a fishing licence – each morning, stamped with the day’s date and a one‑hour allowance. When a villager comes back with the log of their timer reading, the Log‑Keeper will check that the recorded time does not exceed one hour. If a villager’s timer shows more than an hour, the Log‑Keeper will immediately remove that person’s licence and give them a notice: a 24‑hour suspension. During that suspended day the villager is not allowed to set a line on the lake. Because we need one unit of fish to survive each day, a 24‑hour suspension is practically a death sentence – the community will consider it a serious violation and will enforce it by preventing that villager from accessing the shared fishing spots, perhaps with the help of the elders or the village chief. The licence can be reinstated only after the villager has proved compliance: the Log‑Keeper will issue a new licence the following morning after the suspension period has passed.

We keep a simple ledger – a wooden board on the dock – where each villager records the start and end time of their fishing. The Log‑Keeper checks this ledger every evening, verifies the timers, and notes any breaches. The community is expected to discuss any disputes at the village meeting; if a villager contests a suspension, the Log‑Keeper will present the timer evidence, and the elders will decide if the suspension should be upheld or reduced. The 24‑hour suspension thus carries the weight of both losing access to fish for a day and the social stigma of breaking the agreed rule.
